title: GitHub Increased Instant Navigation from 4% to 22% by Rethinking Client Side Architecture
gist: GitHub rebuilt the navigation architecture behind Issues around client-side caching, predictive prefetching and service workers, lifting instant navigations from 4% to 22% and cutting P10 latency from about 600ms to 70ms. Commentary on the piece argues the transferable lesson is shell-first render with cache-hit hydration — not prefetching, which only pays on small read-heavy data graphs like Issues.

insights.claim: GitHub raised the share of instant navigation experiences in GitHub Issues from 4% to 22% by moving work client-side via caching, predictive prefetching and service worker-based request handling.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Even a well-resourced rewrite only made about one navigation in five instant, which calibrates realistic expectations for local-first web migrations.
insights.locator: GitHub has redesigned the navigation architecture

insights.claim: GitHub adopted a local-first approach that renders available data immediately from the browser while background processes retrieve newer information, using IndexedDB for persistent storage plus in-memory caching for frequently accessed data during active sessions.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Layered browser storage (durable plus session-scoped) is the concrete implementation shape of local-first web apps — a pattern replicable in any read-heavy SaaS UI.
insights.locator: To reduce these repeated network dependencies

insights.claim: GitHub's caching follows a stale-while-revalidate model, displaying locally stored data on revisit without waiting for a server response and then background-synchronising to restore consistency with backend data.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Trading strict freshness for immediate render is the explicit product decision behind every perceived-latency win; teams with strong consistency requirements cannot copy it.
insights.locator: The caching model follows a stale-while-revalidate approach

insights.claim: GitHub added preheating — using observed navigation patterns to populate cache entries before users request the data — and service workers that intercept browser requests to serve local resources, falling back to the backend only for unavailable or stale data.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Prediction plus interception is where the instant-navigation gains actually come from, and it requires behavioural telemetry most teams do not collect.
insights.locator: GitHub introduced preheating to improve cache effectiveness

insights.claim: The redesign required GitHub to accept displaying some content immediately and updating it asynchronously rather than waiting for the latest server state on every interaction.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The freshness-versus-responsiveness trade-off is the architectural decision that gates whether a local-first rewrite is even viable for a given product surface.
insights.locator: The architecture required balancing responsiveness with data freshness

themes.theme: What actually transfers to other applications

insights.claim: Commentary on GitHub's work argues prefetching only pays when the data graph is small and read-heavy, because larger graphs with read/write collisions cause prefetched views to re-fetch after landing.
insights.speaker: BareStack
insights.so_what: Read/write collision density is the screening test for whether a prefetching investment will pay back — most enterprise apps fail it.
insights.quote: Prefetching pays when the data graph is small and read-heavy like Issues. Most applications have a larger graph with read/write collisions, so prefetched views may re-fetch after landing.
insights.locator: BareStack highlighted an important distinction around prefetching

insights.claim: The reusable pattern from GitHub's redesign is shell-first render plus cache-hit hydration, not prefetching itself.
insights.speaker: BareStack
insights.so_what: Separates the cheap, broadly applicable half of the architecture from the expensive, narrowly applicable half — a direct prioritisation rule for frontend platform roadmaps.
insights.quote: The reusable pattern is the shell-first render + cache-hit hydration, not prefetching itself.
insights.locator: BareStack highlighted an important distinction around prefetching

insights.claim: GitHub's gains were concentrated in the fast end of the distribution: P10 navigation latency fell from roughly 600ms to 70ms and P25 from 800ms to 120ms, while P90 improved only from 2,400ms to 2,100ms.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Client-side caching moves the head of the distribution, not the tail — teams whose complaints come from the P90 will not get relief from this architecture.
insights.locator: GitHub measured improvements across navigation latency distributions

insights.claim: Median navigation latency at GitHub Issues fell from about 1,200 milliseconds to 700 milliseconds, and P75 from 1,800 to 1,400 milliseconds.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A ~500ms absolute improvement across the middle of the distribution is the honest headline number behind the more marketable 4%-to-22% instant-navigation claim.
insights.locator: P10 latency decreased from approximately 600 milliseconds

insights.claim: Commentators singled out GitHub's shift from optimising the p99 tail to optimising distribution quality as the sign of engineering maturity in the work.
insights.speaker: Oguz Guven
insights.so_what: A reframing of performance targets away from tail SLOs toward whole-distribution shape, which changes what performance teams are measured on.
insights.quote: Shifting from the p99 tail to distribution quality is the real engineering maturity here.
insights.locator: Oguz Guven also pointed out another important performance lesson

insights.claim: A GitHub senior software engineer argues latency should be treated as a cognitive cost — a context switch for the developer — rather than as a measurement.
insights.speaker: Alexander Lelidis
insights.so_what: Framing latency as lost developer focus is how performance work gets funded against feature work; useful language for anyone justifying infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: Latency isn’t just a metric. It’s a context switch.
insights.locator: Alexander Lelidis, senior software engineer at GitHub, explained
